Overdose deaths in Laredo are down so far this year, Dorado Public Health officials reported at an Oct. 15 health meeting — and staff credited a Narcan distribution network that now reaches 10 sites, including a 24-hour location and a vending machine, along with outreach partnerships, with keeping that number low. That account comes from AI-generated meeting summaries from citizenportal.ai, which covered the Oct. 15 session.

The numbers behind the good news

The reported decline is the latest chapter of a longer, documented fall. Laredo's overdose deaths dropped from 36 in 2024 to 15 in 2025, according to a January KGNS report, and DEA Special Agent in Charge Robert Kennedy told the station that fentanyl deaths alone fell from roughly 73 in 2023 to 42, then to 15. Local naloxone distribution has been aggressive: public-health staff reported 84 Narcan boxes distributed in just the first two months of 2026, after roughly 1,300 in 2025 and about 1,200 in 2024, according to AI-generated meeting summaries from citizenportal.ai. Local overdose calls for service fell from 454 to 233 in 2025, per a coalition presentation covered by the same source.

Still, a note of caution: the year-to-date figures are preliminary, and final cause-of-death classifications can lag. Whether the 2026 decline holds will depend on data that has not yet been finalized.

The Narcan network

The 10-site figure has been consistent across meetings — a July coalition session also described naloxone distribution through ten community sites, per citizenportal.ai summaries. The most visible piece of the infrastructure is the harm-reduction vending machine at Laredo Fire Station #3, which offers 24/7 access to Narcan, hygiene kits and fentanyl test kits; it was made possible by $1,196,880 in federal funding for PILLAR's Project PAW through a SAMHSA grant, according to Rep. Henry Cuellar's office. In March, Webb County commissioners weighed installing additional Narcan vending machines, including one inside the Webb County Jail, KGNS reported.

Regionally, Behavioral Solutions of South Texas serves as the distribution hub for the Be Well grant covering 19 counties including Webb; regional coordinator Megan Perez told the county Drug and Alcohol Commission that a probation-office vending machine was being used so heavily it needed weekly restocking, and that her program supplies free naloxone, bulk training and installation help to clinics, school districts and community partners. The Laredo Drug and Alcohol Coalition has also voted to fund a social-media video campaign to normalize Narcan use and show residents how easy it is to grab a kit from a cabinet or vending machine, according to AI-generated summaries from citizenportal.ai.

What's at risk

The same Oct. 15 session carried a warning alongside the celebration. Presenters reported that prehabilitation and detox programs screened and admitted dozens of people in September and described a juvenile referral to rehab — and then flagged that the community has lost a female-specific facility, with funding cited as the barrier to restoring those services, according to AI-generated summaries from citizenportal.ai.

The funding scare behind that worry is recent and concrete. In January, the Trump administration's brief cancellation of $2 billion in federal mental health grants left Laredo providers scrambling: PILLAR co-founder Manuel Sanchez said his organization stood to lose more than $1 million a year, and Webb County's DWI and Juvenile Drug Court director Victor Vasquez said the loss would have slashed $1.3 million from his budget, KGNS reported. The grants were reinstated within a day, but Sanchez told the station he would diversify funding so the organization never faces that position again.

There is also momentum in the other direction: on Sept. 29, PILLAR was awarded a new $2.1 million, five-year SAMHSA grant for its Community in Motion 2.0 project targeting youth ages 12–17 and their families. Webb County Judge-elect Jerry Garza, who takes office Jan. 1, called the expansion of local detox and rehabilitation facilities "a long-overdue priority for the county."

What we're watching

  • Data or reporting? The decline mirrors a national supply shift — the DEA reports the share of lab-tested pills containing fentanyl dropped from 76 percent in 2024 to 29 percent in 2025. Is Laredo riding weaker fentanyl, wider Narcan access, enforcement, or some mix? Nobody at the meeting put a number on each factor.
  • Who tracks whether it holds? Dorado Public Health maintains a public GIS map of overdose hotspots, and the county Drug and Alcohol Commission has asked for quarterly reporting to measure reach across agencies. The final 2026 count — and whether the decline survives year-end — has yet to be published.
  • Where do women in crisis go now? Roots Recovery Center previously told commissioners that an uptick in women seeking detox is straining its capacity, and that pregnant patients need protocols it cannot provide without expanded funding, per AI-generated summaries from citizenportal.ai. With a female-specific facility now gone and funding the stated barrier, the women who would have used it have no clear alternative on the record.

The numbers say Laredo is saving lives. The capacity behind them says the margin is thin.

excerpt: Overdose deaths in Laredo are down year to date, with Dorado Public Health crediting a 10-site Narcan network and outreach partnerships. But the same meeting flagged a lost women-only facility and a funding gap — raising the question: who keeps the decline alive?
title: Overdose Deaths Are Down in Laredo. What's Behind the Drop — and What Could Undo It
